summary: This RFC explains how Explicit Congestion Notification can be used with RTP over UDP, with RTCP as the feedback. It defines a new RTCP XR block, a new RTCP transport feedback message, and a STUN extension for optional initialization.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers can gently signal that the road is getting crowded before dropping packets. This lets video and voice calls hear that signal and slow down.

questions: how to use ecn with rtp
how does rtp detect ecn path failure
subtitle: How real-time audio and video over UDP can hear routers' congestion marks and slow down before packets are dropped.

tldr.problem: ECN lets routers mark packets instead of dropping them, but UDP has no feedback channel and RTP has no handshake, so RTP over UDP could not use it.
tldr.mechanism: Receivers report ECN-CE marks back to the sender using a new RTCP feedback message and a new RTCP XR summary block. SDP attributes negotiate support, and three initiation methods (RTP/RTCP, STUN with ICE, leap of faith) check that the path passes ECN.
tldr.outcome: A sender treats a congestion mark like packet loss and keeps watching for paths that clear or drop ECN marks, falling back to non-ECT traffic if they do.

today: RFC 6679 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows it has been updated by RFC 8311. Read the two together.

sections.title: Why RTP Over UDP Needs Its Own ECN
sections.content:
Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN, RFC 3168) lets a router mark a packet to signal congestion instead of discarding it. TCP, SCTP and DCCP have been updated to carry that signal back to the sender. UDP-based transports such as RTP (RFC 3550) had no specification, because UDP itself has no feedback mechanism. For RTP, that feedback has to come from RTCP.

RFC 6679 defines how. The solution has feedback of ECN-CE marks over RTCP, verification of ECN end to end, and procedures for starting ECN use. Because starting depends on how the session is signalled, it also includes SDP signalling.

The RFC explains why RTP differs from TCP: there is no in-band handshake, feedback normally arrives every few seconds rather than every round trip, congestion response can be quite different from TCP, RTP uses mixers and translators, and it supports multicast. Real-time media benefits especially because packet loss is highly visible to users, while TCP simply retransmits. With ECN, the application can choose how to reduce quality instead of concealing unpredictable loss.

The RFC sets six requirements, including: negotiate ECN before sending ECT packets, feed back every CE mark, limit cheating, detect and fall back from paths that clear or drop ECT, and avoid adding setup time or clipping the start of media.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can put a small flag on a packet that says "it is getting busy here". Phone and video calls needed a way to carry that flag back to the speaker so the speaker can talk a little less.

sections.title: How the Pieces Fit Together
sections.content:
The RFC splits the solution into four parts: negotiating the capability, initiating and verifying ECN, ongoing use, and failure detection with fallback.

Negotiation happens in session signalling. Even if everyone claims support, a middlebox such as a firewall may block packets with ECN bits set, so the sender must verify the path. It can do this in three ways: RTP and RTCP probing, an extra STUN check during ICE, or a leap of faith. The first works in all RTP sessions and is the mandatory-to-implement method.

Once ECN is verified or assumed, the sender marks its RTP packets as ECT. Receivers send quick RTCP ECN feedback when they see CE marks, and also put a regular XR ECN Summary Report in each compound RTCP packet. Cumulative counters let the sender work out what happened even if some RTCP packets are lost.

RTCP packets MUST NOT be ECT marked, because RTCP reports what happened to the ECT traffic and must still arrive when ECT packets do not.

The RFC requires the RTP/AVPF profile (RFC 4585) or one that inherits its rules, for timely feedback, unless a receiver-driven congestion control makes timely feedback unnecessary. Even then it is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: First the two sides agree to use the flags. Then they test that the flags really get through. After that, the listener keeps telling the speaker how many "busy" flags showed up.

sections.title: The Two RTCP Report Formats
sections.content:
The RFC adds two RTCP extensions that carry the same counters in different packing.

The RTP/AVPF transport-layer ECN feedback packet is for urgent news, mainly the arrival of an ECN-CE marked packet. It uses FMT=8 with PT=RTPFB=205. Its report holds the extended highest sequence number, then counters for ECT(0), ECT(1), ECN-CE, not-ECT, lost packets and duplicates.

The RTCP XR ECN Summary Report is for regular reporting and continuous checking. It uses block type BT=13 and carries the same counters for each media sender (SSRC) but omits the highest sequence number, since the SR or RR in the same compound packet already has it. The block length is 5*n words for n report entries; receivers MUST discard reports whose block length is not a multiple of five. If no sender is currently active, the block is still sent with zero length to show the receiver can report ECN information.

The ECT(0) and ECT(1) counters are 32 bits. The ECN-CE, not-ECT, lost and duplicate counters are 16-bit fields that wrap after 65535, so implementations should keep longer local values. Counters start at 0 for each new SSRC. Lost packets and duplicates are counted separately, which differs from the loss counter in RFC 3550, where a duplicate can hide a loss.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of notes the listener can send back. One is a quick note that says "busy flag seen right now!". The other is a regular summary with tallies of everything that arrived.

sections.title: Signalling ECN Support in SDP
sections.content:
The RFC defines a media-level SDP attribute, a=ecn-capable-rtp:, which lists initiation methods in decreasing order of preference: rtp, ice and leap. Unknown methods and parameters MUST be ignored. It has two optional parameters:

  • mode: setread (the default), setonly or readonly, saying whether the endpoint can set ECN bits, read them, or both. If both sides are setonly or both are readonly, there is no common capability.
  • ect: the preferred marking, 0 (the default), 1 or random. Using ECT(0) is RECOMMENDED.

In offer/answer, the offerer lists methods and the answerer replies with a single choice. If the answerer drops the attribute, ECN MUST NOT be used in either direction. In declarative SDP, such as multicast, the attribute includes a single method, and participants MUST NOT join unless they can handle it. The attribute MUST NOT be used for RTP over TCP, SCTP or DCCP.

Two more SDP pieces round this out: the ecn parameter of a=rtcp-fb ... nack for the feedback packet, and ecn-sum in a=rtcp-xr for the summary block. An ICE option, rtp+ecn, goes in a=ice-options when the ICE method is offered. A system using SDP MUST implement the attribute and both parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the game starts, the two sides trade notes saying how they can use the flags: can they put flags on, can they read flags, or both. They only play if their notes fit together.

sections.title: Starting ECN and Running It
sections.content:
All participants on the same transport MUST use the same initiation method. When both in-band and STUN methods are signalled, the sender SHOULD offer ICE with higher priority.

RTP and RTCP (mandatory). The sender marks a small fraction of packets as ECT and leaves the rest unmarked, so media still works if the path blocks ECT. It is RECOMMENDED to send at least two ECT packets per RTCP reporting interval. Receivers answer with ECN feedback and summary reports. The sender treats group membership as stable after at least three RTCP reporting intervals and a full interval without changes. Initiation succeeds when all known participants report correct receipt. For unicast, the sender MAY declare provisional success after one receiver reports success, while continuing to watch for other participants. It has failed if a receiver's RR shows it should have received more than 3 ECT packets but no ECN report arrives.

STUN with ICE (optional). After a candidate is nominated, an extra connectivity check carries an ECT-marked STUN packet with an ECN-CHECK attribute. The server echoes the ECN field it saw in a not-ECT reply. The client is RECOMMENDED to retransmit at least 4 times and give up MAX(1.5*RTT, 20 ms) after the last one. This method only suits unicast destinations.

Leap of faith (optional). The sender goes straight to ongoing use and relies on failure detection. It is only recommended for controlled environments where the whole path is known to support ECT, and NOT RECOMMENDED where ECN-blocking middleboxes may exist, since recovery can take several tens of seconds.

Ongoing use. Once ECN is working, the sender SHOULD mark all RTP data packets, ECT(0) unless told otherwise, but never RTCP. A receiver that sees a CE mark or a loss MUST schedule an RTCP ECN feedback packet as soon as possible, unless timely feedback is not required. The default reaction to a CE mark MUST be to treat it as if packet loss had occurred. The RFC describes sender-driven, receiver-driven (for example dropping a layer of layered video) and hybrid congestion control.
sections.plainLanguage: At first the speaker puts the flag on just a few messages, as a test. If the listener reports the flags arrived safely, the speaker uses them on everything and slows down whenever it hears about a busy flag.

sections.title: Detecting Broken Paths and Falling Back
sections.content:
A path can change so that it includes a node that is not ECN-compliant. Such a node may drop packets marked ECT or CE, which is the worse case, or reset the mark to not-ECT. Senders MUST keep monitoring ECN after initiation for this reason.

The counters make this checkable. The ECT, CE and lost counts should match what the sender sent, allowing for duplicates. If the mix drifts towards not-ECT, the path is clearing marks. If ECT packets are delivered at a noticeably lower rate than not-ECT ones, once CE marks are counted as losses, ECT packets are being dropped. The sender must check that the difference is statistically significant.

A sender seeing high loss on ECT-marked packets SHOULD immediately switch to not-ECT to see whether the losses stop. If they do, it goes back to initiation. If re-initiation fails, it can retry periodically or renegotiate to disable ECN, and disabling is RECOMMENDED if full use has repeatedly fallen back after successful initiations. Failures should be logged.
sections.plainLanguage: If the flagged messages suddenly start disappearing, the speaker stops using flags for a bit to see if that fixes things. If it does, the flags were the problem.

sections.title: Topologies, Translators and Mixers
sections.content:
The RFC goes through the RTP topologies of RFC 5117. Point-to-point works like other unicast transports. Multicast is allowed if the sender has verified the paths to all its known receivers, which is conservative and does not scale to large groups. A video-switching MCU SHALL NOT be used with ECN. The asymmetric mixer/translator topology is NOT RECOMMENDED.

A transport translator that does not modify the media SHOULD copy ECN bits unchanged and pass RTCP through. A translator that combines or splits packets must handle marks as RFC 3168 describes: a combined packet is CE marked or dropped if any input was CE, and RTCP counters are scaled by the ratio of translated to original packets. A transcoder or a mixer splits the control loop in two: it generates its own feedback upstream and MUST NOT forward downstream ECN feedback upstream.

On the implementation side, the standard Berkeley sockets API pre-dates ECN and does not provide what is needed to read or set ECT bits on UDP, so the specification is hard to implement portably.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone in the middle passes your messages along, they have to be careful with the flags. Some just copy them, and others start their own separate conversation on each side.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker who can modify traffic or inject false RTCP can report lots of CE-marked packets to force the sender to its lowest bitrates, or change counters so the sender disables ECN. The defense is to integrity protect the feedback and authenticate the sender. Feedback exposes the receiver's perceived loss and CE marks, which is mostly not sensitive; if it is, RTCP should be encrypted. An on-path attacker can rewrite ECT into CE, a denial of service endpoints cannot defend against on their own.

Signalling can be attacked by removing the ECN attributes, which needs authentication and integrity protection of the signalling. Misbehaving parties are also covered: a receiver may fail to report CE marks to get a larger share, though it risks loss and delay itself, or a receiver may claim to be non-ECN-capable to stop others in a multi-party session using ECN. The RFC leaves out the ECN nonce because a cheating receiver could simply claim not to support it. SRTP, IPsec and DTLS can provide the needed protection, and for SIP the RFC suggests at least SIPS (SIP over TLS) for hop-by-hop protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could shout "busy! busy!" falsely to make the speaker go quiet, or hide the flags to get more room. Locking the notes so no one can change them helps stop that.

fields.name: Extended Highest Sequence Number
fields.desc: Highest RTP sequence number to which this report relates.

fields.name: ECT (0) Counter
fields.desc: Cumulative RTP packets received with ECT(0) from this SSRC.

fields.name: ECT (1) Counter
fields.desc: Cumulative RTP packets received with ECT(1) from this SSRC.

fields.name: ECN-CE Counter
fields.desc: Cumulative ECN-CE marked packets; wraps after 65535.

fields.name: Lost Packets Counter
fields.desc: Expected packets minus received non-duplicate packets.

fields.name: Duplication Counter
fields.desc: Cumulative duplicates of already received packets.
